blocks.prompt: The Dinosaur With a Roof on Its Back
blocks.text: Stegosaurus was a dinosaur. It lived long before any people did. It was as heavy as an elephant, and it walked on four legs. Its back legs were long. Its front legs were short. That made its head hang low, close to the plants it liked to eat. Two rows of tall plates stood along its back. The plates were not paired. They sat in a zigzag. At the end of its tail were four long spikes. If a hungry dinosaur came too close, Stegosaurus could swing that tail. Its head was small. Its brain was about the size of a lime.

blocks.prompt: Why It Is Called the Roofed Lizard
blocks.text: In 1877, a scientist named Othniel Marsh unpacked a crate of huge bones from Colorado. Inside were flat plates of bone, wide as dinner plates and thick as bricks. Marsh thought they had lain flat across the animal's back, overlapping like tiles on a roof. So he named it Stegosaurus, which means roofed lizard. He was wrong about the roof. Better skeletons later showed that the plates stood straight up along the back in two rows, and the rows did not match. A plate on the left sat in the gap between two plates on the right. Nothing else in the fossil record is built quite like it. The plates were not part of the skeleton. They grew inside the skin, the way a crocodile's bumpy scales do. The biggest ones were about two feet tall. Stegosaurus kept its head low and ate ferns and other soft plants. Its brain was small, about the size of a lime, in an animal that weighed as much as an elephant. The name stuck, even though the roof did not.

blocks.prompt: What Were the Plates For?
blocks.text: Stegosaurus is easy to draw and hard to explain. Seventeen bony plates ran along its back in two staggered rows, and after nearly 150 years of study, scientists still argue about what they were for. The first idea was armor. It fails quickly. The plates were thin, hollow in places, and full of channels for blood vessels. They stood upright, leaving the animal's sides exposed. A predator would simply walk around them. The second idea was temperature control. Blood moving through all those channels might have released heat on a hot day, or soaked up warmth in the morning sun, the way an elephant's ears do. This idea was popular for decades. Then researchers compared Stegosaurus to its relatives and found plates in many shapes, some far too small or too narrow to shed much heat. The channels, it turned out, are what you would expect in any bone that grew fast. The idea that fits best now is display. Different kinds of stegosaur had differently shaped plates. That is what you see in animals that need to recognize their own kind, or to look large and impressive to a rival. A plate cannot stop a bite, but it can make a five ton animal look even bigger. Defense was not neglected. It was moved to the other end. Stegosaurus carried four spikes on its tail, each up to three feet long, and the tail was flexible enough to swing hard. We know it swung. One Allosaurus fossil has a hole punched through a tail bone that matches a Stegosaurus spike exactly, and roughly one spike in ten shows damage from use.

blocks.prompt: The Thagomizer, and Other Things We Got Wrong
blocks.text: Stegosaurus has been misunderstood since the day it was named. In 1877, Othniel Marsh gave it a name meaning roofed lizard because he pictured its plates lying flat across its back like shingles. Articulated skeletons later proved the plates stood upright in two staggered rows, seventeen of them, and no living animal wears anything quite like them. The name was already permanent. The second mistake was more embarrassing. Marsh noticed that the spinal canal in the hip region swelled to many times the volume of the animal's actual brain, which was roughly the size of a lime in a body as heavy as an elephant. He proposed a second brain back there, a hip brain to run the rear half of the animal. The idea was too good to die quietly, and it appeared in children's books for a century. Birds have a similar swelling, and it holds a glycogen body, a store of energy that has nothing to do with thinking. Stegosaurus almost certainly had one brain, and a small one. The tail spikes got the strangest fix of all. Paleontologists had no name for the four spike arrangement at the end of the tail. In 1982, a newspaper cartoonist named Gary Larson drew a caveman lecturing with a pointer at a diagram of a spiked tail, labeling it the thagomizer, after the late Thag Simmons. Paleontologists liked it. They started using it in talks, then in papers. The joke is now the working term. The spikes themselves are the least uncertain thing about the animal. Ken Carpenter and colleagues described an Allosaurus tail vertebra with a puncture that matches a Stegosaurus spike in shape and size, and roughly one spike in ten shows breakage or infection from impact. A Stegosaurus plate has been found bitten in a way that matches Allosaurus jaws. These two animals met, and it did not always go well for the predator. What remains genuinely unsettled is the plates. Armor does not fit the evidence. Temperature control has weakened. Display leads. After a century and a half, the most famous feature of one of the most famous dinosaurs is still an open question.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Stegosaurus stenops, about 150 million years ago
Morrison Formation: Colorado, Wyoming, Utah
17 osteoderm plates, staggered in two rows
Thagomizer: four spikes, named from a 1982 cartoon
Sophie: 85 percent complete, on display in London since 2014
Lived about 83 million years before T. rex

blocks.prompt: The Roof That Was Never a Roof
blocks.text: Begin with the time. Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago, in the Late Jurassic, on a warm floodplain that is now Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah. Tyrannosaurus rex lived about 67 million years ago. The gap between them is roughly 83 million years, which means Stegosaurus was more ancient to T. rex than T. rex is to us. The two never met and never could have. The toy box that puts them in the same fight is off by a span of time longer than the entire age of mammals. Deep time is the first thing this animal teaches, and most people never learn it. Now the name. In 1877, Othniel Charles Marsh received bones from Colorado in the middle of the Bone Wars, his bitter race against Edward Drinker Cope to name more species than his rival. Speed was the point, and speed costs accuracy. Marsh saw broad, flat plates of bone and assumed they had lain across the back in an overlapping sheet, like tiles. He called the animal Stegosaurus, roofed lizard, and moved on. He was wrong. When an articulated skeleton came out of the Colorado rock in the 1880s, the plates were standing upright in two rows, and the rows were staggered, each plate filling the gap opposite it. The roof was never a roof. The name is permanent anyway, because scientific names do not get corrected for embarrassment. Then the plates themselves, which are still not solved. There were seventeen of them, the largest around two feet tall, and they were osteoderms: bone grown within the skin rather than attached to the skeleton, which is why they scatter after death and why early reconstructions guessed wrong. Armor is the obvious reading and the weakest. The plates were thin, they left the flanks unprotected, and one plate has been found bearing bite damage that matches Allosaurus jaws, which tells you they could be bitten. Thermoregulation held the field for decades. The plates are threaded with grooves for blood vessels, so perhaps they dumped heat the way an elephant's ears do. That idea has thinned. Comparisons across stegosaur species turned up plates of many shapes, including some far too small to work as radiators, and the vascular grooves are ordinary features of fast growing bone. Display leads now, precisely because plate shape varies so much between species. A structure that differs species by species is usually a signal, not a tool. Defense lived at the other end. Four spikes projected from the tail, each up to three feet long, on a tail flexible enough to swing with force. The evidence that they were used is unusually direct: an Allosaurus vertebra punctured by a wound matching a Stegosaurus spike, and roughly one spike in ten showing fractures or signs of infection from impact. The apparatus has a formal sounding name, the thagomizer, which paleontologists borrowed in earnest from a 1982 Gary Larson cartoon in which a caveman points to a diagram and credits the arrangement to the late Thag Simmons. The field had no term. A joke supplied one. It is now in the literature. The animal carrying all of this had a brain roughly the size of a lime and a beaked mouth of small leaf shaped teeth that could not chew. It cropped ferns and low plants and swallowed them nearly whole, five tons of animal running on a head held about three feet off the ground. The best specimen we have, an eighty five percent complete skeleton nicknamed Sophie, went on display in London in 2014 and is still being studied. Almost 150 years after Marsh guessed at a roof, the most recognizable dinosaur on Earth is still turning in its answers late.
